meta.title: 3I/ATLAS Just Got Weirder... and a Radio Signal From 63 Light-Years Away

lines: Something ancient just flew through our solar system, and the more we look, the stranger it gets.
Astronomers now say this interstellar comet may be ten billion years old.
And at the same time, a radio signal from sixty-three light-years away has the internet asking one question.
Is it aliens?
Stay with me, because the real answer is even more fascinating.
In July twenty twenty-five, a NASA-funded telescope in Chile, part of the ATLAS survey, spotted a faint dot moving far too fast to be one of ours.
Its orbit was a hyperbola, an open curve that never loops back. That is the signature of an object from interstellar space.
It became only the third interstellar visitor we have ever confirmed, after Oumuamua in twenty seventeen, and Borisov in twenty nineteen.
Racing at roughly one hundred thirty-seven thousand miles per hour, it was also the biggest and brightest of the three.
Its icy core is estimated at somewhere between four hundred meters and five and a half kilometers across.
Here is its route through our neighborhood.
Around October twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-five, it reached perihelion, its closest point to the Sun, about two hundred and three million kilometers out, just inside the orbit of Mars.
For weeks it hid behind the Sun, invisible from Earth.
Then, on December nineteenth, it made its closest approach to Earth, a safe distance of about two hundred seventy million kilometers.
No threat. But a perfect chance for every major telescope to take a look.
Webb, Hubble, and spacecraft around Mars and Jupiter all turned to watch.
And that is where it got weird.
After rounding the Sun, 3I/ATLAS brightened dramatically, and turned bluer.
Astronomers then imaged at least seven jets of gas and dust streaming out in different directions.
Some pointed toward the Sun, forming what look like anti-tails.
Its motion also showed a small push beyond gravity, which comets can do when gas vents from the surface.
That fueled wild headlines. Harvard's Avi Loeb even floated the idea of artificial thrusters.
But NASA says the comet behaves like a natural one. No unexplained slowdowns, no course changes. Right where gravity says it should be.
A weird comet, yes. A spaceship? No.
Then the James Webb Space Telescope took a look.
In December twenty twenty-five, as the comet moved away from the Sun, Webb's infrared spectrograph read its chemical fingerprint.
The results, published in Nature in June twenty twenty-six, are unlike any comet in our solar system.
First, deuterium, also known as heavy hydrogen. 3I/ATLAS has about thirty times more of it than comets born around our Sun.
That kind of heavy water ice only survives if it stays deeply frozen, and never gets long-term warmth.
Second, carbon. Compared to solar system comets, 3I/ATLAS has far less of the heavy isotope, carbon thirteen.
Carbon thirteen builds up over time, as generations of stars live and die. Less of it means an earlier, more pristine galaxy.
Put those clues together, and you get a stunning age.
Researchers estimate 3I/ATLAS formed ten to twelve billion years ago, during what astronomers call cosmic noon, when star formation in the universe was at its peak.
Our Sun and planets are only about four and a half billion years old. This comet may be more than twice as old.
The universe itself is thirteen point eight billion years old, so this visitor is nearly as old as time itself.
One April study even suggests it may have been born before its own star.
Its exact age is still an estimate, but researchers say it is almost certainly older than anything we have from our own solar system.
Now the comet is outbound, never to return.
But another story from deep space is making headlines.
And this one involves radio waves, from sixty-three light-years away.
In a preprint posted on September fifteenth, astronomers reported something no one had confirmed before.
Radio waves coming directly from a planet outside our solar system.
The planet is Beta Pictoris b, a young gas giant about ten to twelve times the mass of Jupiter, orbiting a star sixty-three light-years away.
The team used MeerKAT, an array of sixty-four radio dishes in South Africa.
And this was not a one-off. They recorded repeating bursts, at multiple frequencies.
Crucially, they traced the emission to the planet itself, not the star it orbits. That has been the big hurdle for earlier searches.
It is the first direct detection of radio emission from an exoplanet.
So what is making the signal?
Auroras. Just like Earth's northern lights, but on a monstrous scale.
Charged particles spiral along the planet's magnetic field and produce radio waves, the same way they do at Jupiter.
To reach the frequencies detected, the field has to be incredibly strong. At least two hundred times stronger than Jupiter's.
Beta Pictoris b spins once every eight to nine hours, which may help power it.
Harvard's Edo Berger acknowledged that radio signals make people think of the search for extraterrestrials.
But the team is clear: this is evidence of a colossal magnetic field, not intelligent life.
Earlier alerts, like the Wow signal in nineteen seventy-seven, or a twenty fifteen blip from a star ninety-four light-years away, never turned into confirmed messages.
Two stories: an ancient comet from a vanished era, and a planet broadcasting in radio.
Neither is aliens. Both are real science rewriting what we know.
Subscribe, and tell me in the comments which one blew your mind more.
A comet older than our Sun. A radio signal from another world.
3I/ATLAS brightened, turned blue, and sprouted at least seven jets. NASA says it is natural.
Webb found thirty times more heavy hydrogen than solar system comets.
That points to a birth ten to twelve billion years ago. Before our Sun existed.
Meanwhile, MeerKAT caught radio waves from a planet sixty-three light-years away.
Aliens? No. It is a magnetic field two hundred times Jupiter's.
Follow for more space science.
